activities.caption: true or false — what each traversal guarantees
activities.name: gpLoopJudge

statements.s: BFS and DFS are the same loop with different containers, so either one finds shortest paths.
statements.why: Only BFS exhausts distance d before d+1 — its first arrival is provably a shortest unweighted path; DFS dives and may arrive by a long route first.

statements.s: DFS's job is structure — cycles, topological order, connected components.
statements.why: A back edge to a node still on the stack means a cycle; finish-time order reverses into a valid task sequence.

statements.s: Topological ordering is the algorithm behind build systems and course prerequisites.
statements.why: DFS's finish-time order reversed is a valid task sequence.

statements.s: BFS needs a weighted graph to promise shortest paths.
statements.why: The ring property holds in unweighted graphs — or weighted with equal weights; costs are Dijkstra's territory.

activities.anchor: The table cost 4 × 6 = 24 cells instead of 16
activities.caption: call the brute-force bill for twenty items
activities.name: gpKnapsackEst

config.prompt: Brute force over a knapsack with twenty items checks every subset. Roughly how many is that?
config.why: 2²⁰ ≈ a million possibilities — the DP grid replaces it with 20 × capacity entries: exponential becomes polynomial.
config.context: For the capacity-5 miniature, two dozen entries against sixteen possibilities.

activities.anchor: Knowing which regime you are in is the design skill
activities.caption: walk the method choice for a new problem
activities.name: gpRegimeBranch

config.root: A new problem lands on your desk. Walk the method choice.

start.text: Can a local choice be provably safe — is the cheapest edge crossing any partition always part of some optimum?

choices.label: Yes — greedy it is
choices.feedback: Kruskal and Prim territory: faster than DP, applicable to fewer problems — local safety holds, so no grid is needed.

choices.label: No — but best answers compose from best subproblems that recur
choices.feedback: Both ingredients hold: dynamic programming — cache each subproblem once and the exponential tree collapses to a grid.

choices.label: Top-down — keep the recursion, add a cache
choices.feedback: Memoisation: only reachable subproblems are computed — better when the state space is sparse.

choices.label: Bottom-up — fill the grid in dependency order
choices.feedback: Tabulation: no call overhead, compiler-friendly, and the space trick becomes visible.

greedy.text: Greedy confirmed. But test it — if local safety ever fails, the greedy answer is confidently wrong.

choices.label: Local safety fails sometimes — fall back
choices.feedback: That boundary — between provable local safety and the need for a grid — is the discipline.

topdown.text: Sparse state spaces love memoisation — you pay only for states you actually visit.

bottomup.text: Dense, performance-critical grids love tabulation — and the previous-row trick shrinks memory to a single row.

fallback.text: Exact DP up to a size, approximation for provable near-answers, heuristics for good-enough — the professional spectrum.

config.why: Greedy, DP or brute force — the choice is testing whether local choices are safe, not reaching for a favourite.

config.prompt: Kruskal at work on the miniature — put the steps in order:
items: Sort the edges by weight: AB=1, AC=2, DE=2, BC=3, CD=5, BD=6
Consider BC (3) — it would cycle A-B-C: skip
Tree complete at weight 10: four edges for five vertices — the n−1 shape
config.why: Both greedy algorithms are provably optimal — the cut property — which is exactly why these are not DP problems.

activities.anchor: keeps the order but not contiguity
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the recurrence behind git diff
activities.name: gpLcsCloze

config.text: LCS("ABCDE", "ACE") = "ACE", length %%0%% — the shared letters in sequence, gaps allowed. If the last characters match, take %%1%% + LCS(i−1, j−1); otherwise max(LCS(i−1, j), LCS(i, j−1)). For two 5,000-letter genomes the grid holds %%2%% million cells.
config.hint: git diff, DNA alignment, spell-check — one recurrence, three industries.

activities.anchor: no recursion overhead, friendlier to memory limits
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the fill-order detail
activities.name: gpFillSpot

config.prompt: A summary of the two DP styles contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Memoisation keeps the recursive structure — write the natural recurrence, add a cache.
Top-down only computes reachable subproblems — an advantage when the full grid is not needed.
Tabulation fills the grid in dependency order — no call overhead.
The knapsack row only needs the previous row, so iterate forwards to avoid reusing an item twice.
The fill order IS the correctness argument: each cell depends only on cells already final.
config.correction: Iterate BACKWARDS, to avoid reusing an item twice — that single careful direction collapses the grid from O(n × capacity) to O(capacity) memory.
config.why: Choose top-down when the recurrence is intricate or the state space sparse; bottom-up when dense and performance-critical.
